# Draft:Edward DeMille Campbell House

The Edward deMille Campbell House, also known as the Campbell/Hays House, is a house and historical landmark located at 1555 Washtenaw in Ann Arbor, Michigan. The house was constructed in 1899 and designed by renowned Michigan architect Albert Kahn for University of Michigan chemistry professor Edward deMille Campbell and his family. The house received a preservation award from the Ann Arbor Historic District Commission in 2012. As of 2012, it is owned by Holde and Robert Borcherts, who purchased the property in 1979.
There is another house that is sometimes referred to as the Edward deMille Campbell House in historical records, but is located down the street on 1310 Hill. This was the residence of the Campbell family before they moved to 1555 Washtenaw. This house was eventually sold to Margaret Lydecker, who opened it as a boardinghouse. Lydecker's daughter, Margaret Wolaver, eventually sold the house to then-University of Michigan basketball coach David Strack. Strack sold the home to Haskell and Janet Newman in 1972.
Edward deMille Campbell
Campbell was born on September 9, 1863 in Detroit. He was the son of Cornelia Hotchkiss and James Valentine Campbell, a justice of the Supreme Court of Michigan who became the first dean of the University of Michigan Law School. After initially demonstrating interest in zoology, Edward Campbell decided to study chemistry, specializing in metallurgy. In 1888, he married Jennie M. Ives, the sister of Martin Ives, a soap manufacturer who lived in an Ann Arbor neighborhood that would later be dubbed Ives Woods. Jennie and Campbell would go on to have six children and seven grandchildren. In 1890, he became an assistant professor of metallurgy, teaching courses in quantitative analysis, assaying, and metallurgy.
In the spring of 1892, when he was twenty-eight years old, Campbell was doing research on the causes of the hardening of steel. He was conducting an experiment involving fractional combustion when the instrument he was using exploded, blinding him permanently. Following his accident, Campbell reconfigured his research process, utilizing assistants who were often undergraduate students. During the course of his career, he published twenty-three research papers in analytical chemistry, forty papers on the properties of steel, and fourteen on Portland cement. Campbell died on September 18, 1925.
History
The land on which the Campbell House was built was originally a farm owned by J.D. Baldwin. Baldwin sold part of the land in 1859 to Henry Simmons Frieze, who then sold the land to J. Austin Scott. The land was divided into six lots in the 1890s, one of which became the land on which the Campbell House now stands.
After the chemical explosion in 1892, Campbell sought to live in a residence that was specifically designed to help him move around. Kahn designed the home in a Georgian classical revival style, incorporating interior woodwork, roomy stairways, and porcelain keyholes and door handles.
Campbell and Ives' six children inherited the house when their parents died in the 1920s. In 1929, one of the children, Mary Lavinia Ives Campbell, bought out her siblings with her husband, James Griffith Hays. They renovated the house while still aiming to preserve key elements of Kahn's design. It is one of the only Kahn-designed houses remaining in Ann Arbor.
In 1979, the Hays family helped create a Washtenaw/Hill Historic District Study Committee, established in order to propose that their house and several surrounding properties be part of a historic district in Ann Arbor.
